column4: The source section names root خ ش ع for lowered faces; 70:44 again gives humbled eyes and surrounding humiliation on that day, matching 88:2.
The source's خ ش ع face detail returns with eyes lowered and disgrace; 68:42 supplies the failed call to prostrate, so this verse shows abasement after a rejected summons.
The wrongdoers stand exposed to the Fire, خَاشِعِينَ مِنَ الذُّلِّ; this directly joins the source's bowed face to humiliation before punishment.
At resurrection eyes are خُشَّعًا as people leave their graves like scattered locusts; the scene repeats the lowered gaze of 88:2.
The day of trembling hearts has eyes خَاشِعَةٌ; the source's lowered-face root thus appears again in the bodily fear of judgment.
On the day people follow the caller, voices are خَشَعَتْ to the Merciful; this carries the source's lowering from faces into the sound of the gathering.
The source connects a high garden and lowly faces; 56:3 names the Hour as خَافِضَةٌ رَافِعَةٌ, the day that lowers some and raises others.
The source identifies root ع ل و in the high garden; 69:22 uses the same phrase, جَنَّةٍ عَالِيَةٍ, in a parallel description of the Garden.
After its high Garden, 69:23 says its fruit is دَانِيَةٌ, near at hand; height and accessible low-hanging provision coexist in one scene.
The source's raised couches use root ر ف ع; 56:34 describes the Garden's beds as مَرْفُوعَةٍ, a close furniture parallel.
Recliners rest on lined couches while the fruit of the two Gardens is near; this develops the source's elevated seating with bounty brought within reach.
The source places أكواب low in a Garden where people sit high; 43:71 has golden dishes and cups circulated among the people, showing vessels as service for their occupants.
Here silver vessels and أكواب are carried around the Garden's people; the source's set cups and raised couches become a fuller serving scene.
The people of the Garden receive cups, pitchers, and a cup from a flowing spring; it repeats the source's cup imagery as provision.
The earlier Garden group reclines on woven سرر; this adds a parallel elevated-seat scene to the source's raised couches.
The righteous recline on arranged couches in the Garden, repeating the source's human place of honor above the placed cups.
The Garden's shade covers its people and its fruit is made readily accessible; the low reach of the fruit complements the source's high Garden and raised seating.
God shields people from that day's evil and gives them نَضْرَةً وَسُرُورًا; this contrasts the source's humbled faces with the Garden's radiant, joyful outcome.
80:38 begins the other face-scene with radiant faces on that day, setting the Garden's ease beside the source's lowered faces.
Those radiant faces laugh and rejoice in 80:39; it fills out the opposite outcome to the source's abasement.
80:40 turns to other faces on that day, now covered with غَبَرَةٌ; the paired faces echo the two outcomes surrounding 88:2.
Those faces are covered by قَتَرَةٌ in 80:41, completing the dark, constricted counterpart to the source's raised Garden scene.
80:42 identifies these grim-faced people as the disbelieving sinners; it makes the face-contrast a judgment of response, not just appearance.
75:22 gives radiant faces on that day, a positive counterpart to 88:2's humbled faces.
The radiant faces in 75:22 look toward their Lord in 75:23; this adds their stance to the source's contrast between abasement and Garden honor.
75:24 turns to other faces, بَاسِرَةٌ, on that same day; the passage again divides faces into opposite outcomes.
Those faces expect a back-breaking disaster in 75:25, clarifying why the source's lowered face belongs to a punitive scene.
The righteous look out from الأرائك in 83:23; this repeats the source's elevated resting place in a Garden.
Their faces show نَضْرَةَ النَّعِيمِ in 83:24, a bright-faced contrast to the source's humbled faces.
Those punished are told they will eat from the tree of زَقُّوم; this parallels the source's Hell-side thorn food.
The condemned fill their bellies from that tree in 56:53, giving the source's food that cannot relieve hunger a more explicit counterpart.
The meal is followed by الحَمِيم in 56:54, matching the source's hot spring and punitive provision.
They drink like parched camels in 56:55; this makes thirst persist after the source's food fails to relieve hunger.
The tree of زَقُّوم is named as the food of the sinner in 44:43, a direct Hell-food parallel to the source.
44:44 says this is طَعَامُ الأَثِيمِ, specifying the condemned eater as the source's Hell-food scene does.
The food boils like molten substance in the belly in 44:45, intensifying the bodily suffering attached to the source's thorn food.
The address ذُقْ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَزِيزُ الْكَرِيمُ mocks the condemned person's claimed greatness; the source's dictionary root ك ب ر also carries self-aggrandizement, now answered by punishment.
For the condemned there is no food except غِسْلِين in 69:36; this repeats the source's deprivation through a different Hell food.
69:37 restricts that food to sinners, completing the source's distinction between punitive and Garden provision.
The Hell-dwellers taste neither coolness nor drink in 78:24; this clarifies the deprivation behind the source's food that cannot satisfy hunger.
Their only drink is حَمِيم and غَسَّاق in 78:25, a close counterpart to the source's boiling spring.
The people of the left are in scorching wind and boiling water; this repeats the source's hot, exposed punishment scene.
56:43 adds shade of black smoke, extending the environment surrounding the source's Hell food and heat.
That shade is neither cool nor beneficial in 56:44; the verse reinforces the source's absence of relief.
The Garden group receives chosen fruit in 56:20, the provision-side counterpart to the source's Hell food.
They also receive bird meat as desired in 56:21; this sets satisfying Garden food beside the source's unsatisfying meal.
The Garden's people are supplied with fruit and meat in 52:22, reinforcing the source's contrast between provision and deprivation.
The blessed are told to eat and drink in enjoyment for what they sent ahead; this ties Garden provision to deeds, against the source's punitive food.
Garden fruit is repeatedly provided in 2:25; that abundant provision clarifies the opposite of the source's food that cannot ease hunger.
The promised Garden has lasting food and shade in 13:35; this gives the source's high Garden a sustained-provision counterpart.
After a dispute over food, the people are struck with ذِلَّةٌ and misery; this concretely joins the source's low-food/abasement association while showing refusal of provision ending in humiliation.
When provision is widened, the person says رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ; the verse exposes the self-ranking by material plenty that the source warns against in its height-and-pride turn.
When provision is restricted, the person says رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ; this directly joins food provision to claimed abasement, then the following verses correct that inference.
The verse says God gives honor and ذِلَّةٌ to whom He wills; it makes the source's raised status the Lord's gift, not a height a person claims for himself.
The source names root ر ف ع for raised couches; in a gathering where people are told to rise, God يَرْفَعِ the believers, making elevation a divine gift.
God apportions livelihoods and يَرْفَعُ بَعْضَهُمْ فَوْقَ بَعْضٍ دَرَجَاتٍ; this gives the source's high place a worldly parallel as an allocated rank.
The source's root ر ف ع appears in the good word that ascends and the righteous deed God يَرْفَعُهُ; height here follows worshipful action rather than self-exaltation.
The verse says Idris was raised to مَكَانًا عَلِيًّا; it combines the source's raising root with a high station given to a person.
God is رَفِيعُ الدَّرَجَاتِ and sends warning of the meeting day; this places true height with the Lord who grants it.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the foundations of the House in 2:127; the source's root ر ف ع also names an upward act, here used for a sacred structure.
The source's root ر ف ع is used for houses God permits to be raised; here elevation marks a consecrated place where His name is remembered.
The source's dictionary note for root ض ر ع includes abasement; 6:42 uses يَتَضَرَّعُونَ for people whom hardship might bring to humble supplication.
When punishment arrives, 6:43 asks why they did not يَتَضَرَّعُوا; it turns the source's link between abasement and suffering into a missed chance to humble oneself.
The same root ض ر ع appears when hardship is sent to a town so its people might يَضَّرَّعُونَ; this repeats abasement as a response to distress.
Despite punishment, people do not humble themselves to their Lord or تَضَرَّعُوا in 23:76; it repeats the source's root while showing resistance to the abasement meant to turn them back.
The source's root ض ر ع also names humility; 7:205 tells the listener to remember and call the Lord تَضَرُّعًا and fearfully, a chosen posture rather than the source's imposed abasement.
The source uses root خ ش ع for faces humbled on judgment day; 23:2 calls believers خَاشِعُونَ in prayer, showing chosen humility before the forced lowering of 88:2.
Here help comes through patience and prayer and is easy only for the خَاشِعِينَ; 2:46 supplies their expectation of meeting and returning to God, linking chosen humility to judgment.
The verse asks whether believers' hearts should خَشَعَتْ to God's remembrance; the source's humbled face is an imposed end-state, while this is a requested, living response to God.
Some People of the Book are described as خَاشِعِينَ لله while believing revelation; this uses the source's humility root for reverence rather than humiliation.
The servants of the Merciful walk on earth هَوْنًا; this embodied lowliness contrasts with self-given elevation and the humility imposed in the source's judgment scene.
The verse forbids turning one's cheek away in contempt and walking proudly on earth; it makes bodily haughtiness the chosen inverse of the source's lowered face.
The proud walker cannot split the earth or reach mountains in height; the source's root ع ل و has a self-exalting branch, and this verse sets an explicit limit on it.
All creatures in the heavens and earth prostrate without arrogance; the source's warning about self-assigned height is bounded by the posture of creation before God.
People are made nations to know one another and the most honored before God is the most mindful; this replaces self-awarded rank with a measure from God, like the source's granted Garden elevation.
The verse sets العَذَابَ الأَدْنَىٰ before العَذَابِ الأَكْبَرِ; this directly matches the source's reading of the greater punishment against a lesser, earlier stage.
The condemned enter النَّارَ الْكُبْرَىٰ; the source itself cites this earlier surah's phrase as another use of the root ك ب ر for the greatest punishment.
87:16 says people prefer الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا; this supplies the low, nearer-life choice behind the source's contrast between granted Garden height and punishment.
The next verse says the Hereafter is خير وأبقى; it completes the boundary between preferred near life and the lasting outcome tied to the source's high Garden and great punishment.
The one who transgresses and آثَرَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا is the source of the low-life choice set against the raised Garden.
For that transgressor, Hell is the refuge in 79:39; it gives the source's self-elevating turn its punitive destination.
The one who fears standing before the Lord and restrains the soul from desire is the contrasting figure to the source's self-aggrandizing person.
For the restrained soul, the Garden is the refuge; this makes the source's high Garden a granted outcome of fear and restraint.
The source's dictionary root ع ل و includes arrogant self-exaltation; Pharaoh's claim أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ is its sharpest self-awarded height.
The next verse says God seized Pharaoh as a warning for this life and the next; it completes the source's movement from claimed height to punishment.
Iblis is said to have اِسْتَكْبَرَ; the source's dictionary root ك ب ر includes self-greatening pride, and this refusal turns elevation into rebellion.
The question أَسْتَكْبَرْتَ أَمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الْعَالِينَ joins pride to being among the high; it directly echoes the source's two branches for ع ل و and ك ب ر.
Iblis says he is better because he was made from fire and Adam from clay; this states the self-ranking behind the source's warning about height claimed by a person.
The command فَاخْرُجْ مِنْهَا orders Iblis out after his pride; it makes the fall from self-claimed rank explicit.
Pharaoh is called لَعَالٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ; the source's dictionary branch for root ع ل و names arrogant domination, and this is its worldly instance.
God turns signs away from those who act arrogantly on earth without right; this applies the source's self-exalting sense of ع ل و to a refusal of guidance.
Pharaoh's people reject signs despite inward certainty, ظُلْمًا وَعُلُوًّا; the source's highness-to-arrogance branch fits this self-raised stance.
Those too proud to worship enter Hell دَاخِرِينَ; the source's root ك ب ر self-aggrandizement ends in the humiliation opposed to its raised Garden.
39:60 joins darkened faces with the home of the مُتَكَبِّرِينَ; it fuses the source's lowered face and its warning about pride.
The Hereafter's home belongs to those who do not desire عُلُوًّا in the land or corruption; this makes the source's Garden elevation a gift for those who refuse self-elevation.
The person who turns away and اِسْتَكْبَرَ displays the source's secondary ك ب ر sense; 74:26 supplies the threat of Saqar, while this verse contributes the arrogant response.
Saqar is the punishment announced after the arrogant rejection in 74:23; this verse supplies the fire-side consequence to the source's great-punishment link.
The source names root ر ف ع and the sky's height; 79:28 says God raised its ceiling and proportioned it, a direct cosmic raising.
After describing the raised heaven, 79:30 says the earth was spread; this gives the source's high sky and low earth their paired scene.
God رَفَعَ the heaven and وَضَعَ the balance; the source names both raising and placing roots for couches and cups, and this verse pairs their opposite actions.
The earth is وَضَعَهَا for living beings in 55:10; it gives the source's raised sky and low-placed furnishings a grounded counterpart.
The verse makes earth a bed and heaven a canopy for people, the same below-and-above arrangement the source draws from earth and sky.
God makes earth a settled place and heaven a structure; this repeats the source's visible lower-ground/upper-sky relation.
The built sky is above the people in 50:6; 50:7 completes the view with the spread earth, matching the source's vertical pair.
50:7 says the earth was spread and set with mountains and growth; 50:6 supplies the sky above it, completing the source's cosmic contrast.
The heaven is built with power in 51:47; 51:48 completes the image with the earth spread, recalling the source's raised heaven and lower earth.
The earth is spread in 51:48; its paired sky-building in 51:47 supplies the above counterpart to the source's cosmic arrangement.
Seven heavens are created in layers in 71:15; this gives the source's raised sky a visible vertical structure.
God makes the earth بُسَاطًا for people in 71:19; this supplies the lower, traversable counterpart to the source's layered heavens.
God makes earth مِهَادًا in 78:6; the later heavens above in 78:12 complete a lower-ground/upper-sky arrangement like the source's.
78:12 describes seven strong heavens above people; 78:6 supplies the earth made a resting place, completing the source's vertical pair.
The sky is called السَّقْفِ الْمَرْفُوعِ, a raised roof; this repeats the source's raising image beyond its raised couches.
God رَفَعَ the heavens without visible pillars in 13:2; this is another direct instance of the source's raising root in the sky.
God raised some messengers over others in degrees; this repeats the source's raised-status root as an act assigned by God.
God says He raises whom He wills in degrees; Abraham's story supplies a human status that comes from God, like the source's gifted height.
In Joseph's story God says نَرْفَعُ دَرَجَاتٍ مَّن نَّشَاءُ; it repeats the source's raising root for rank given by God.
God says He will رَافِعُكَ إِلَيَّ to Jesus; this is a personal elevation attributed to God rather than self-claim.
The command to let man look at his food opens a provision scene; it sets the source's Hell food against food's ordinary dependence on what God brings forth.
Water is poured out in 80:25; it adds the needed source of nourishment beside the source's boiling spring.
The earth is split open in 80:26 so food can grow; this connects the source's spread-earth scene to sustenance rather than the Hell-side barrenness.
Grain is made to grow in 80:27; this contrasts ordinary nourishment with the source's thorn food.
Grapes and fodder follow in 80:28; the sequence shows food and pasture as provision unlike the source's non-nourishing meal.
Olives and palms in 80:29 extend the cultivated food provision that contrasts with the source's deprivation.
Gardens are densely grown in 80:30; the verse adds the fruitful landscape absent from the source's Hell scene.
Greenery and pasture in 80:31 continue the provision list, contrasting with the source's non-nourishing food.
The growth is a provision for people and livestock in 80:32; this states explicitly what the source's Hell food fails to provide.
